form.4. COURSE INTENT:
Central question the course answers: How can software developers effectively
design and operate development workflows in which humans and AI agents
collaboratively build reliable software?

Pedagogical emphasis: Practical, workflow-oriented understanding through
hands-on development and experimentation.

This course should NOT become:
- A general introduction to AI or machine learning
- A traditional programming course
- A purely theoretical treatment of large language models

labs.title: Introduction to Agentic Coding Environments
labs.exercise: Set up the local development environment and explore the APIs of common AI-assisted coding tools, verifying connectivity and listing configuration parameters.
labs.notes: Focuses on environment readiness and initial API verification.

labs.title: Model Context Protocol Configuration
labs.exercise: Configure Model Context Protocol (MCP) server settings and tool permissions within VS Code, ensuring integration matches the provided interface specification.

labs.title: Context Engineering and Prompt Protocols
labs.exercise: Implement and test context engineering protocols to optimize prompt context for MCP-enabled tools, verifying tool execution against specifications.
labs.notes: Deepens MCP configuration with prompt protocols.

labs.title: Analyzing Requirements Ambiguities
labs.exercise: Analyze a supplied informal software project requirements document, identifying and documenting at least five ambiguities or contradictions using an AI assistant.
labs.notes: Prepares students for formal specification translation.

labs.title: Gherkin Feature File Generation
labs.exercise: Translate informal user stories into executable Gherkin feature files using AI assistance, covering all specified use cases for the target project.
labs.notes: Translates domain-specific requirements into structured formats.

labs.title: Tracing Agent Execution Logs
labs.exercise: Trace execution logs and loop outputs generated by an AI coding agent on a buggy implementation, mapping out the control flow paths.
labs.notes: Focuses on understanding agent control loops.

labs.title: Aider Agent Trace Analysis
labs.exercise: Analyze execution traces from an Aider coding agent for a buggy Python function, identifying and documenting three distinct failure causes with log evidence.
labs.notes: Prepares students for debugging agent-generated code.

labs.title: Mid-Semester Catch-up and Open Lab
labs.exercise: No new lab content. Students use this session to catch up on previous lab exercises, refine their MCP configurations, and prepare for mid-semester evaluations.
labs.notes: Mid-sem exam week. No new content introduced.

labs.title: Evaluating Copilot Generated Test Suites
labs.exercise: Generate unit test suites using GitHub Copilot for a given module, evaluate their reliability, and justify decisions against requirements.
labs.notes: Focuses on evaluation and testing reliability.

labs.title: Architecting AI-Native Workflows
labs.exercise: Design and document a unified workflow plan, integrating tool workflows and context engineering protocols for a multi-component application.
labs.notes: High-level architectural planning for the capstone.

labs.title: Capstone Integration and Workflow Setup
labs.exercise: Set up and integrate the end-to-end AI-native software development workflow for a supplied microservice module, preparing for live evaluation.
labs.notes: Initial capstone integration and environment setup.

labs.title: Live Workflow Evaluation and Walkthroughs
labs.exercise: Demonstrate the AI-native workflow live, executing three scenario walkthroughs chosen by the evaluator to evaluate execution performance.

labs.title: Final Project Review and Submission
labs.exercise: Finalize all project deliverables, document performance evaluations, and submit the complete workflow repository.
labs.notes: Final wrap-up and submission of the capstone project.

tutorials.activity: Interactive walkthrough of setting up API keys, configuring environment variables, and testing basic LLM API calls in Python.

narrative.course_description: This course examines modern AI-native software development, focusing on how developers collaborate with coding agents. Designed for third- and fourth-year students, the curriculum addresses how to define intent, engineer context, structure iterative development workflows, and coordinate AI tools. Students will learn to configure agentic coding tools and context protocols for development environments, and translate informal system requirements into executable specifications. Additionally, they will analyze execution traces and loop outputs of AI coding agents to diagnose software failures, and evaluate the reliability of agent-generated test suites. Finally, students will evaluate end-to-end AI-native software development workflows. The course is taught through three hours of lectures, one tutorial hour, and two hours of practical laboratory sessions per week, complemented by a substantial hands-on development project.
narrative.sequencing_rationale: The course sequence progresses logically from foundational tool configuration to complex integration. It begins with agentic tools and context engineering in Module 1, builds to requirements translation in Module 2, moves to trace analysis and debugging in Module 3, covers automated testing evaluation in Module 4, and culminates in a capstone workflow integration in Module 5. Desirable prerequisite CSE201 ensures students possess the necessary object-oriented programming, collection frameworks, and unit testing background to engage with these advanced modules.
narrative.assessment_rationale: The assessment mix balances theoretical understanding and practical application. The midsem (20%) and endsem (25%) exams evaluate conceptual knowledge of requirements engineering, trace analysis, and reliability. Hands-on skills are heavily weighted through labs (15%), assignments (15%), and a major project (25%), aligning directly with the course's practical focus. This structure ensures students can configure tools, analyze agent loops, and demonstrate end-to-end workflows in live scenarios as required by the course outcomes.
narrative.positioning_rationale: This course is complementary to existing IIIT-D offerings. Unlike CSE701, which focuses on data-driven software engineering and repository mining, this course emphasizes practical workflow engineering. It differs from CSE581's focus on traditional and agile design theories by centering on AI-driven executable specifications. While CSE582 targets legacy system maintenance, this course addresses AI-native development loops. Finally, it expands on the algorithmic agent focus of CSE594A by providing a comprehensive, 4-credit treatment of software development workflows.
